# Data & Methods

# Data Description

For this research, the dataset of the Michigan Residential Community Survey was used. This survey
was used to evaluate the Michigan Learning Communities and focussed, among other things, on the
social satisfaction of their first-year students. For the sake of this course, only the data of one
of the programs was used, from the first cohort (2022-2023). The pre-survey (Wave 1) could be
answered from October 19 to November 19 and the post-survey (Wave 2) could be answered from March
3th to April 10th.

This specific program contained 121 students who answered at least one of these surveys. The
response rate for the first wave was 91,474% and for the second wave it was 94,21%. Eleven students
only answered the questions of the second wave and thirteen students only answered the questions of
the first wave.

## Variables

**Hanging out**

The 'hanging out' variable is the network variable used for this study. For the second hypothesis,
this variable is the dependent variable, for the third and fourth hypothesis, it is an independent
variable. The question asked for this variable was 'Which students in your MLC do you hang around
with and talk to the most?'. Students could nominate up to ten of their fellow students.

For the students that only participated in one of the two waves, it meant that if they were
nominated by their fellow students anyways, this was still coded as a non-nomination (0), because
they did not consent to participating in that specific wave. Additionally, their own nominations
(which was an NA), were also coded as 0. This means that there could be some bias in the network
structures.

**Social satisfaction**

Social satisfaction is the dependent behaviour variable for the second and third hypothesis. Five
questions were asked to measure the social satisfaction of the students. As two of these questions
were asked as a negative (I feel left out of things, I am lonely), only the three positive questions
(I have made some good friends at the U of M, I am happy with my friends at the U of M, I like how
my social life is going this year) were taken into account for the sake of this course. Answers were
proposed on a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). The average of these three
positives was taken to measure the social satisfaction of students.

**Covariate: Parental Education Level**

Parental education level is one of the independent variables for the first and third hypothesis.
Students had to answer what the highest education level was for both of their parents. For this
study, these responses were first binary coded for both of the parents. If the highest education the
parent had completed was 'trade/technical/vocational training' or less than this, the response was
coded as 0, anything above that was coded as 1. Followingly, responses for parent 1 and parent 2
were taken together. If at least one of the parents had completed higher education, the variable was
coded as 1 for the student.

**Control variables**

To account for the influence of other factors on the hypotheses, gender and ethnicity were taken
into account as control variables.

# Methods

## Descriptives

As my first research question is about whether segregation based on parental education level occurs
on the macro-level, I will look at two relevant segregation statistics for this: Coleman's homophily
index and Moran's I. Additionally, I am interested in reciprocity, so I will also look into what
that looks like for both of the waves and I will also report how many mutual dyads have occurred.
Lastly, for some basic descriptives, the number of ties will be reported, as well as the density of
the network in both waves.

## Explanatory

I have done the exploratory analyses by making use of the Stochastic Actor-Oriented Models (SAOMs)
with RSiena [@ripley2025].These model the evolution of network structures and in this case, also the
behaviour of the agents. It does this through estimating 'rules' for the agents on how they change
their ties or behaviour. These rules can be seen as the micro theory of action. Into my RSiena
model, structural effects, covariate effects and behavioural effects have been taken into account.
For each hypothesis, there are a couple of effects that will be taken into account.

**Research question 2**

The second research question aims to estimate to what extent reciprocated friendships occur between
students whose parents have the same educational level and whether this is significant. For this
model, I include sameX and sameXRecip and because the underlying mechanisms for sameX are egoX and
altX, these were initially included as well.

The egoX variable takes into account the likelihood that ego gets a tie if it has a certain
covariate. The altX variable assesses the chance that ego sends a tie to an alter with a certain
covariate, regardless of ego's covariate. SameX then looks at how many of the ties that ego has send
out to alter, have exactly the same value on their covariate [@ripley2025]. So, in this case, sameX
looks at if a student whose parents have attended higher education, has send out ties to, for
example, four people, how many of those ties are send to people whose parents have also attended
higher education. sameXRecip, followingly, then looks at how many of the reciprocated ties that ego
has, are with an alter that has the same covariate as them [@ripley2025].

**Research question 3**

The third research question looks into the extent to which reciprocated ties between students have a
positive effect on social satisfaction. For this model, I included RecipDeg and avRecAlt. The
RecipDeg effect takes into account what the effect is of reciprocated relations on behaviour, the
behaviour in this case being social satisfaction. The avRecAlt effect controls for the influence
that alter's behaviour has on ego, by looking into the extent that ego is influenced by the people
to whom it has a reciprocated tie. It takes ego's behaviour and multiplies it by the average
behaviour of his reciprocated alters [ripley2025].

**Research question 4**

The last question builds on to the mechanism analysed in question 3, but then taking into account to
what extent having a same covariate, in this case having parents with the same educational level,
plays a role in the effect of the reciprocated tie on behaviour, in this case, social satisfaction.
For this question, the effects avSameXRecAlt and avRecAltSameX are taken into account.

The avSameXRecAlt effect looks into what the influence is of reciprocated ties between the same
covariate on behaviour, meaning, in this case, what the influence is of a reciprocated tie between
students whose parents have the same educational level, on the student's social satisfaction. The
avRecAltSameX takes into account the average social satisfaction of all alters whose parents have
the same educational level as ego, to whom ego has a reciprocated tie [ripley2025]. This effect thus
also controls for the influence of alter's behaviour on ego, but with taking into account whether
ego and alter have the same covariate or not.

**Model Construction**

The construction of the first model resulted from a process of trial-and-error. After checking a
couple of Goodness-of-Fit distributions (see the RCode-section in the exploratory results), it turns
out that the model with the most statistics seemed the best, although the Goodness-Of-Fit
distribution is still significant, indicating that the model does not fit very well. The additional
effects included were the gwespFF effect, which accounts for transitivity, the indegree-popularity
effect, the outdegree-activity effect and the out-isolate effect. Perhaps other control variables
would have made the model better, but I also do not want to face the risk of over-controlling.
